title: a word for wishing well on people you don't like
hook: a word for wishing well on people you don't like
tomorrow: the whole first instruction: in, out

segments.voice: The coworker who replies all. The neighbor with the leaf blower at seven on a Saturday. The relative with opinions about your life at every holiday. Not villains. Just people who are hard to like. Maybe a face comes to mind already. Now here's an old Buddhist practice: people sit quietly and wish that person well. On purpose. Not because they've forgiven anything, and not because the person has earned it. Just as training, the way you'd train a muscle. It sounds almost backwards. Buddhists trace it to the Buddha's own teaching. Today, the word for it.
screen: `THE ONE WHO REPLIES ALL.` → `NOW WISH THEM WELL.` → `ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: Metta. It's a word in Pali, the old language the Buddha's teachings were kept in. It comes from mitta, a friend. So metta is friendliness. A wish for someone's good, the plain warm kind you'd feel for a friend, pointed at anyone at all. You may know its Sanskrit cousin, maitri, or the name Maitreya, the friendly one, the Buddha that tradition says is still to come. There's a short teaching on metta, the Metta Sutta, still chanted in Buddhist homes and monasteries. It pictures a mother protecting her only child with her own life, and says to hold a heart like that toward every living being. Seen and unseen. Near and far. Born and not yet born. Every one. That's the size of it. And the Buddha's own verses put the reason bluntly. In Max Müller's old translation of the Dhammapada: "hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love—this is an old rule." An old rule. Not a new idea even then. How do people actually do it? Later teachers laid out a gentle order. Start with yourself, because it's hard to give what you've never felt. Then someone you love. Then someone neutral, the person who sells you coffee. Then, last and slowest, someone difficult. You don't pretend to like them. You just wish them what you'd want: to be safe, to be well, to be at ease. Some who practice it describe an odd side effect: it changes them more than anyone else. The difficult person is still difficult. They just carry less of that person around.
screen: `METTA — FROM MITTA, A FRIEND.` · `LIKE A MOTHER WITH HER ONLY CHILD.` · `HATRED CEASES BY LOVE.` · `YOU, A FRIEND, A STRANGER, THE HARD ONE.` · then, large: `MAY YOU BE AT EASE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice for day one, and it's small on purpose. One breath, with the bell. Bring back that face from a minute ago. You don't have to feel warm. Breathe in slowly. And on the way out, let a few words go toward them, out loud or just inside: may you be at ease. That's all. One breath of friendliness, pointed somewhere unusual.
Metta. Friendliness. A wish for anyone's good, even the people who make it hard. First word on your strand.
screen: `METTA — your 1st word` → clicks onto an empty word-strand.

segments.voice: Your line to carry: may you be at ease. Once today, when someone annoys you, in traffic, in a meeting, in a group chat, say it inside, just once, and notice what happens in you. That's day one. You showed up. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE WHOLE FIRST INSTRUCTION: IN, OUT.`

howItsDone: Buddhists practice metta by silently repeating short wishes, such as may you be safe, may you be well, may you be at ease, first for themselves and then outward to loved ones, strangers, difficult people and all beings; the Metta Sutta is chanted in monasteries and homes.

fork.setup: you're learning metta the traditional way. who do you start with?
options: the most difficult person you know.
fork.reveal: the classic order, set out by the commentator Buddhaghosa, starts with yourself, then a loved one, then a stranger, and only then someone difficult. the hard one comes last, and slowly.

original.note: Pali, written here in Devanagari: friendliness, goodwill. From mitta, a friend. Sanskrit: maitrī.

trapdoor: what you thought: being nice to people.
what it means: a trained wish for anyone's good, from yourself outward to the people who are hard to love.
what a scholar hears: mettā, from mitta, friend. the Karaniya Metta Sutta pictures a mother guarding her only child, and asks for a heart like that toward all beings.
